
# Setting the LILO Password

With LILO you are vulnerable only to single-user mode or booting into an insecure operating system. LILO can be configured to ask for a password before any operating system or kernel on the system is booted. LILO configuration was discussed in Chapter 6.

To configure the LILO global password add the **password=***<password>*** line, where **password** is the new LILO password. You are not hashing the password, so it is plain text in the file. Figure 12-2 shows the /etc/lilo.conf file.

FIGURE 12-2
lilo.conf file.

```
boot=/dev/sda
map=/boot/map
default="linux"
keytable=/boot/us.klt
prompt

nowarn
timeout=100
message=/boot/message
menu-scheme=wb:wb:wb:bw
password=myPassWord03
image=/boot/vmlinuz
	label="linux"
	root=/dev/sda1
	initrd=/boot/initrd.img
	append="devfs=mount acpi=off"
	read-only
image=/boot/vmlinuz
	label="failsafe"
	root=/dev/sda1
	initrd=/boot/initrd.img
	append="devfs=nomount acpi=off failsafe"
	other=/dev/fd0

```

Any time you change /etc/lilo.conf you must run the */sbin/lilo* -v command. This line installs the LILO boot loader and will be activated the next time you boot the system.

# Password Security

By default, during installation, the Linux operating system is set to use MD5 and shadow passwords. These offer secure user verification before allowing access to the system.

Even MD5 passwords can eventually be cracked. If an individual gains access to the system, the /etc/passwd file can be copied to another machine and the passwords it contains can be broken with password cracking programs. If strong passwords are not used, the MD5 passwords can be broken in minutes.
